sentences.text: Petitioner seeks for a direction to permit the goods covered by Ext.P3 Bill of Entry to be cleared for re-export after re-processing, by permitting it to be moved to a customs bonded premises.
2. Petitioner is a manufacturer and exporter of cashew based products.
In the year 2022, 400 cartons of about 8000 Kg of organic cashew kernels were exported by the petitioner.
However, since the foreign buyer rejected the goods due to an alleged mis-match of the label, the goods were re
- imported claiming the benefit of Customs Notification No. 45/2017
. However, the customs subjected the imported goods to certification by the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI).

entities.text: Food Safety and Standards Authority of India
entities.label: ORG

sentences.text: The said Authority rejected 200 cartons of cashew kernels out of the total 400 cartons stating those to be unfit for home consumption.

Subsequently, petitioner amended the Bill of Entry claiming the benefit of Notification No.158/1995 and indicated that they were ready to execute necessary bonds promising to re-export the goods after re-processing.
However, the Commissioner of Customs ordered confiscation stating that the amendment of Bill of Entry was an afterthought.

Challenging the said order of confiscation, petitioner approached the Customs, Export Service Tax Appellate Tribunal, Bengaluru ('CESTAT'), pointing out that since the products have been undertaken to be re-exported and also since the goods are not unfit for human consumption but only that, the standards of FSSAI were not met, nothing prevents them from re-exporting goods after re- processing.

entities.text: Customs, Export Service Tax Appellate Tribunal, Bengaluru
entities.label: COURT

sentences.text: CESTAT allowed Customs Appeal No.20010/2024 by order dated 04-06-2024 and directed the petitioner to re-process the same by dry heating within the premises of the Customs and re-export the goods at the earliest.

While so, since the petitioner found it difficult to carry out dry heating within the customs premises, an application was filed for modification of the order of the CESTAT, to permit the petitioner to carry out the process within the premises of its factory.
However, observing that the Tribunal does not have the jurisdiction to review its own orders, the said application was dismissed.

4. In the meantime, petitioner's factory was designated as a 100% Export Oriented Unit (EOU) on 23.10.2024 with all the permissions from the Customs to treat its premises as a customs bonded premises.
Since petitioner can carry out re-processing work within its own bonded premises, it M/S Tasty Nut Industries vs The Commissioner Of Customs on 3 April, 2025

being designated as a 100% EOU, petitioner has approached this Court, seeking the directions mentioned earlier.

Customs Department has objected to the prayers pointing out that petitioner ought to have approached the Customs Authorities for such permissions and further that, removal of the cargo for re- processing them for re-export require re-assessment of the subject Bill of Entry to provide the benefit of the MFDR notification No.52/2003 and hence the petitioner ought to have approached the jurisdictional Customs Authorities.
6.
I have heard Sri. Adithya Venugopal, the learned counsel for the petitioner as well as Sri. V Girish Kumar, the learned Standing Counsel for the 1st respondent.
7. The consignment of cashew kernels that were ordered to be confiscated has been permitted by the CESTAT order to be re- processed and re-exported.
However, the re-processing to be done through dry heating within customs premises would have practical difficulties.
At the same time, there is the need to ensure that the same products are exported by the petitioner and hence the CESTAT directed the re-processing to be carried out within the customs premises.

8. Concededly, subsequent to the CESTAT order, petitioner's factory has been designated as 100%
EOU and is therefore, now, a customs bonded premises.

All products processed in a 100% EOU can only be exported and therefore, the Department's apprehension that the cashew kernels would be interchanged under the guise of 2025:KER:28623 reprocessing has no basis.

In such circumstances,
even if re-processing is done within the premises of the EOU unit of petitioner's factory, it will be under the watch and care of the Customs Officials as well.

The petitioner's factory having become a customs bonded unit, no reason exists to deny permission to the petitioner to remove the cashew kernels covered by Ext.P3 Bill of Entry to be re-processed in its own customs bonded premises being an EOU.

9. As far as the contention that the petitioner must approach the Customs Authorities, it needs to be mentioned that the CESTAT order already specifies that it should be done within the customs premises.
The Customs Department is bound by the said direction and therefore they would not be able to modify the direction.
Hence, an application to the Customs Authorities by itself without any direction from a superior forum will not suffice the requirement of the petitioner.

In such circumstances, resort to this Court under Article 226 of the Constitution of India, by the petitioner,
is justified.

10. However, since the grant of benefits of MFDR notification No.52/2003 requires the re-assessment of the subject Bill of Entry, the petitioner can be permitted to approach the authorities who shall pass appropriate orders permitting the petitioner to remove the goods from the customs premises to petitioner's 100% EOU unit, which itself is a custom bonded unit, for re-processing and re-exporting.
